A constant real part Relnz=L means ln∣z∣=L, so its level sets are the concentric circles
x2+y2=e2L,L∈R.​

Their radii are strictly positive. The real part is independent of the logarithm's branch, so there is no branch ambiguity in these circles.
For Re(1/z)=K, the equation is x=K(x2+y2). If K=0, complete the square to obtain
(x−2K1​)2+y2=4K21​,(x,y)=(0,0).​

These circles have centres on the real axis and are tangent to the imaginary axis at the excluded origin. Positive K puts the circle to the right, negative K to the left. The separate case K=0 gives the punctured imaginary axis x=0, y=0​. The sketch uses an open marker at the origin to emphasize that 1/z is never defined there.

Set w=ez=0. The hyperbolic cosine equation becomes w+w−1=−4, hence w2+4w+1=0. Its two polynomial roots are w=−2±3​, both negative. Taking every value of the complex logarithm yields
z=ln∣w∣+i(2k+1)π,k∈Z.

Since (2−3​)(2+3​)=1, their real logarithms have opposite signs. All solutions are therefore

The positive real constant is also arcosh2, the inverse hyperbolic cosine of 2. Substitution gives coshz=−cosh(ln(2+3​))=−2 for both signs and every integer k.

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
Assume F is continuously differentiable near the point of interest on F=0, and that the relevant denominators below are nonzero. The total differential on the surface is
dF=Fx​dx+Fy​dy+Fz​dz=0.
(32)
Holding z fixed gives Fx​dx+Fy​dy=0, so the implicit function theorem gives
(∂x∂y​)z​=−Fy​Fx​​,(∂y∂x​)z​=−Fx​Fy​​.
(33)
When Fx​Fy​=0, their product proves the reciprocity rule for constrained partial derivatives:
(∂x∂y​)z​(∂y∂x​)z​=1.​
(34)
Similarly, holding y or x fixed gives (∂x/∂z)y​=−Fz​/Fx​ and (∂z/∂y)x​=−Fy​/Fz​. With Fx​Fy​Fz​=0, multiply the three ratios:
(∂x∂y​)z​(∂z∂x​)y​(∂y∂z​)x​=(−Fy​Fx​​)(−Fx​Fz​​)(−Fz​Fy​​)=−1.​
(35)
This is the cyclic partial derivative identity. Nonzero denominators and local differentiable coordinate representations are substantive assumptions: at a singular coordinate representation, a formal cancellation of zero or infinite factors is not a valid proof.

(∂y∂x​)z​=−yz−Cxz​,(∂z∂x​)y​=−yz−Cxy−C​,(∂z∂y​)x​=−xzxy−C​.​

i OurBigBook.com
There is a global-domain issue in the printed question. Write D=a2x2+b2y2>0 away from the origin. Direct partial differentiation gives
Py​=−D2ab(a2x2−b2y2)​=Qx​.
(38)
Thus the differential one-form is a closed differential form for every real a,b=0. The Poincaré lemma makes it locally an exact differential form on small neighborhoods avoiding the origin. There is no additional condition such as a2=b2.
However, the stated domain is the whole punctured plane, which is not simply connected. To test global exactness, use the closed ellipse x=cost/a, y=sint/b, 0≤t≤2π. Here D=1 and
Pdx+Qdy=ab(xdy−ydx)=dt,∮(Pdx+Qdy)=2π.
(39)
The line integral of a globally exact differential form around any closed curve would be zero. Consequently
globally exact on R2∖{0}: no allowed a,b;locally exact: all a,b=0.​
(40)
The distinction is precisely that of the elliptically scaled angular one-form. The remaining parts can be answered consistently using a local angle branch, as follows.

Solution
Words: 78
ii OurBigBook.com
On a chart with x=0, set
f(x,y)=arctan(axby​)+C.​
(41)
The chain rule verifies both components:
fx​=1+(by/(ax))21​(−ax2by​)=−Daby​=P,fy​=1+(by/(ax))21​axb​=Dabx​=Q.
(42)
A coordinate-independent description of the local potential is a continuous branch of arg(ax+iby), the complex argument of the scaled coordinates. Such branches can also cover points where x=0, using a different angular chart. Continuing once around the missing origin changes that angle by a nonzero multiple of 2π, so there is no global single-valued f on the full stated domain.

The nonzero factor ab/D can be cancelled in the local differential equation, leaving xdy−ydx=0. On an interval with x=0,
dxd​(xy​)=x2xy′−y​=0.
(43)
Hence the explicit general solution is
y(x)=Cx,C∈R,​
(44)
on any interval that avoids the excluded origin. It also follows from fixing the local angle potential, with slope C=(a/b)tan(f−C0​). As parameterized curves there are also vertical rays x=0, which cannot be represented as single-valued functions y(x). Geometrically the connected integral curves are rays, not lines continued through the undefined origin.

For the first-order linear ordinary differential equation, seek an integrating factor M(x) that makes its left side a product rule derivative. Multiplying by M gives My′+MPy, and comparison with (My)′=My′+M′y requires M′=PM. On an interval where P is continuous choose
M(x)=exp(∫x0​x​P(t)dt),M(x0​)=1.
(46)
This factor is never zero. The transformed equation is (My)′=MQ, so integration from x0​ to x yields
y(x)=M(x)1​[C+∫x0​x​M(t)Q(t)dt].​
(47)
Here C=y(x0​) for an initial value problem. The indefinite integral version is y=e−∫Pdx[C+∫Qe∫Pdxdx], with any constant choices inside the integrating factor absorbed into C. Continuity of P,Q is a convenient sufficient hypothesis for a classical differentiable solution of a differential equation.

Since 1+x2>0 for all real x, divide the equation by that factor. Its linear coefficient can be integrated by polynomial division:
P(x)=1+x23x3​=3x−1+x23x​,∫P(x)dx=23​x2−23​ln(1+x2).
(48)
Thus a positive integrating factor is M=e3x2/2(1+x2)−3/2. Multiplying the divided equation gives the product rule form
dxd​(My)=(1+x2)5/26x​.
(49)
The integration by substitution u=1+x2 gives
My=−(1+x2)3/22​+C,y=e−3x2/2[C(1+x2)3/2−2].

The initial condition y(0)=1 fixes C−2=1. The required solution is therefore
y(x)=e−3x2/2[3(1+x2)3/2−2],x∈R.​

No real singularity was introduced by the division or the integrating factor, so the solution extends over the entire real line.

An interior stationary point has vanishing gradient:
∇f(x0​,y0​)=0,fx​(x0​,y0​)=fy​(x0​,y0​)=0.​
(52)
For a differentiable function, this is the necessary first-order condition for an interior local minimum or local maximum.

ii

Words: 155 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 155
ii OurBigBook.com
Write A=fxx​, B=fxy​, C=fyy​ at the stationary point, and let D=AC−B2=0. Under the usual second-order Taylor expansion hypothesis, the second-derivative test gives
D>0, A>0D>0, A<0D<0​strict local minimumstrict local maximumsaddle point​​
(53)
Indeed the quadratic term is (Aξ2+2Bξη+Cη2)/2. For A=0, completing its square gives [A(ξ+Bη/A)2+(D/A)η2]/2. The two coefficients have the same positive sign, the same negative sign, or opposite signs in the respective cases. A negative D also forces the two Hessian eigenvalues to have opposite signs, including the case A=0.
There is a qualification to the printed assumptions: existence of second partial derivatives only at the point does not ensure the needed quadratic approximation. Continuous second partial derivatives in a neighborhood are sufficient. The existence of second partial derivatives does not justify the Hessian test: for example, the function g=x2+y2−6x2y2/(x2+y2) away from the origin, extended by g(0,0)=0, has Hessian 2I at the origin but g(t,t)=−t2 and g(t,0)=t2. Thus the classification above uses the standard additional regularity assumption, which the smooth function in part (b) satisfies.

Put G=(x2+y2)/2+ax4/4, so f=eG>0. Since fx​=fGx​ and fy​=fGy​, its stationary points satisfy
y=0,x(1+ax2)=0.
(54)
The origin occurs for every real a. There are two additional points only for a<0, at x=±1/−a​.
At a stationary point, the Hessian matrix simplifies because ∇G=0:
Hf​=fHG​=f(1+3ax20​01​).
(55)
At the origin this is I, so (0,0) is a strict local minimum for every a, with f=1. If a≥0 it is also the unique global minimum, since G≥0 with equality only there. For a<0, the two extra points have 1+3ax2=−2, so their Hessian has opposite-sign eigenvalues. Thus
a<0: (±−a​1​,0) are saddle points,f=exp(−4a1​).​
(56)
There are no local maxima. When a<0, the origin is not a global minimum: f(x,0)→0 as ∣x∣→∞, but f never attains zero.

y2=2lnL−x2−2x4​.

For a=−1, the contour equation becomes

The central local minimum is surrounded by closed ovals for 1<L<e1/4, accompanied by outer open branches. At L=e1/4, the level passes through the two saddle points (±1,0) and changes its connectivity. Levels L<1 have only outer branches, while levels above the saddle value have an upper and a lower branch. The sketch is restricted to the requested square; labels give G=lnf, so they identify the corresponding contours of f without exponentially large labels.

a OurBigBook.com
A uniformly shuffled deck makes all unordered five-card hands equally likely, giving (552​) possible hands. Choose the rank appearing four times in 13 ways; all four suits of that rank are then fixed. The remaining card can be any of the other 48 cards. No hand is counted twice, because five cards cannot contain two different complete four-card ranks. This use of combinatorics gives the probability
P(four of a kind)=(552​)13⋅48​=(552​)624​,N=624.​
(70)
Here (552​)=2598960 is a binomial coefficient; the probability also simplifies to 1/4165≈0.000240096.

b OurBigBook.com
Assume that wrong-note events are independent events and that each note has the same error probability p, with 0≤p≤1. Then their count N has a binomial distribution. Choose the n mistaken positions in (n100​) ways and multiply the probabilities of the errors and correct notes:
P(N=n)=(n100​)pn(1−p)100−n,n=0,1,…,100.​
(71)
The endpoint cases p=0 or p=1 are understood by continuity, giving deterministic counts. More than half means at least 51 mistakes, so
P(booing)=n=51∑100​(n100​)pn(1−p)100−n.​
(72)
The single-note error probability alone would not determine this count distribution if mistakes were correlated; independence is the additional standard modeling assumption.

A probability density function must be nonnegative. The printed condition s=0 is therefore too weak: for s<0 the given prefactor makes the function negative everywhere. The location-scale form of the logistic distribution requires s>0, which is assumed in the remaining parts.
Set t=(x−μ)/(2s), so dx=2sdt. The normalization of a probability distribution follows from the antiderivative of the squared hyperbolic secant:
∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=21​∫−∞∞​sech2tdt=21​[tanht]−∞∞​=1​.
(73)
For completeness, the same expression with s<0 integrates to −1, since the transformed limits reverse. If a signed scale were desired, replacing its prefactor by 1/(4∣s∣) would give a valid density, but that is a correction to the printed formula.

FX​(x)=21​[1+tanh(2sx−μ​)].

If μ>0, the requested probability is FX​(μ)−FX​(0). Since the hyperbolic tangent is odd, this gives
P(0<X<μ)=⎩⎨⎧​21​tanh(2sμ​),0,​μ>0,μ≤0.​​
(75)
The second case matters because the question places no sign restriction on μ: the event is empty when its upper endpoint is nonpositive. Using an oriented integral from 0 to a negative μ would give a negative number, not a probability.

The same integration by substitution gives the expected value
E[X]=21​∫−∞∞​(μ+2st)sech2tdt=μ+s∫−∞∞​tsech2tdt.
(76)
The remaining integrand is an odd function. Its integral is absolutely convergent, since sech2t≤4e−2∣t∣ and ∣t∣e−2∣t∣ is integrable. Thus cancellation under symmetry in integration is legitimate, rather than merely a principal-value calculation. Consequently
E[X]=μ.​
(77)
Equivalently, the logistic distribution is symmetric about μ, and its exponentially decaying tails ensure that its expected value exists.

A row's squared Euclidean norm is [(1+3​)2+1+(1−3​)2]/6=3/2, and the dot product of the two rows is [2(1−3)+1]/6=−1/2. Thus the row Gram matrix is
AAT=(3/2−1/2​−1/23/2​).​

For the column Gram matrix, the first and third squared column norms are 4/3, the middle one is 1/3, and the respective cross-products are 1/3,−2/3,1/3. Hence
ATA=31​​41−2​111​−214​​.​

The two products are square matrices of different sizes; their unequal dimensions are consistent with A being rectangular.

In ATA, every row sums to one, so (1,1,1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. The antisymmetric direction (1,0,−1) gives eigenvalue 2. A direction orthogonal to both is (1,−2,1), and direct multiplication shows that it lies in the kernel of a linear map. Normalizing all three gives the complete system
σ1​=1σ2​=2σ3​=0​v1​=3​1​(1,1,1)Tv2​=2​1​(1,0,−1)Tv3​=6​1​(1,−2,1)T​​

The original differential equation is defined only where x=0 and y=0. Put w=y3, so the chain rule gives w′=3y2y′. Multiplying the equation by 3y2 yields a first-order linear ordinary differential equation:
w′=2x2+xw​,w′−xw​=2x2.
(93)
An integrating factor on either half-line is 1/x, up to an irrelevant nonzero constant. Equivalently, apply the quotient rule directly:
(xw​)′=xw′−w/x​=2x.
(94)
Integrating gives w/x=x2+C. Thus the real general solution is
y(x)=3x3+Cx​,C∈R,​
(95)
on any connected interval where x=0 and x3+Cx=0. These restrictions preserve both the original denominator and differentiability of the real cube root. In particular C=0 includes y=x on either half-line; this solution has not been lost through division by an expression involving y/x−1.
For verification, differentiating y3=x3+Cx gives 3y2y′=3x2+C, while (2x3+y3)/x=3x2+C. The two sides agree wherever the original equation is defined.

The seven requested parabolas are y=cx2 for c=−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3; the case c=0 is the horizontal axis. Positive c opens upward, negative c downward, and larger ∣c∣ gives a narrower parabola. All pass through the origin with a horizontal tangent line.
To find orthogonal trajectories, use the continuous family y=cx2 containing these seven representative members. Its slope is y′=2cx=2y/x away from x=0. Two finite slopes of perpendicular tangents multiply to −1, so the orthogonal slope is
dxdy​=−2yx​.
(96)
This separable differential equation gives 2ydy=−xdx, hence
x2+2y2=C,C>0.​
(97)
These ellipses are the regular real trajectories; C=0 is a single point, not a regular curve, and C<0 has no real points. One example is x2+2y2=2, with semiaxes 2​ horizontally and 1 vertically.
The implicit tangent relation 2xdx+4ydy=0 also describes points with vertical tangents, where the slope quotient is unavailable. At intersections with the member y=0, the ellipse has a vertical tangent line and is perpendicular to that horizontal axis. The common origin of the parabolas is not on any regular trajectory with C>0. The sketch shows the requested seven members and the example ellipse.
